title: How Zero Sync Works
subtitle: Local-first reads, your own Postgres, and live queries on every platform
throughline: one query, from a React hook down to your own Postgres and back to the screen as a live, always-syncing result

chapters.title: The Local-First Read
chapters.blurb: A useQuery hook reads from a database that lives on the device, so the answer arrives instantly with no fetch.

story.title: The Local-First Read
story.subtitle: Local-first reads, your own Postgres, and live queries on every platform

steps.title: The Local-First Read
steps.narration: Zero is a **local-first** sync engine. A query is answered from an on-device store first; the network is a background detail.
steps.say: Zero starts somewhere surprising. Your data is already on the device, so a read never waits for a server.
steps.coverSubtitle: Your UI reads from a database that lives on the device

steps.title: The UI asks for data
steps.narration: Your component calls **`useQuery`** from `zero-react`. Behind it is the **`Zero`** client (`zero-client`) — a queryable database running in the browser.
steps.say: In a Zero app your interface asks for data through a hook called use query. Behind it sits the Zero client, a small database running inside the browser.

steps.title: ZQL becomes a pipeline
steps.narration: The query is **ZQL** (`z.query.issue.where(...)`). It compiles to an **incremental view** pipeline (`zql/src/ivm`) that maintains its result over time.
steps.say: Your query is written in Zero's own query language, ZQL. The client compiles it into an incremental pipeline that knows how to keep its answer up to date.

steps.title: Reading the on-device store
steps.narration: The pipeline reads from a local key-value store — `IDBStore` (IndexedDB) provided by **Replicache**, the engine `zero-client` uses under the hood.
steps.say: It runs that query against a local store that Replicache keeps in the browser. The rows are right there, no request required.

steps.title: Materializing the result
steps.narration: The view materializes into a **`QueryResult`** — `[rows, { type }]` — where `type` reports whether the result is `complete` or still loading.
steps.say: The pipeline materializes the matching rows into a live result: an array of rows, plus a little detail telling you whether the data is complete.

steps.title: Render, no spinner
steps.narration: `useQuery` returns the result to your component, which renders immediately. Because the data was local, there is *no* loading round trip.
steps.say: That result is handed straight back to your component and it renders. No spinner, no fetch, no waiting.

steps.title: Reads never wait
steps.narration: The local loop: **`useQuery`** → **`Zero`** → **ZQL/IVM** → **Replicache store** → result. Reads are synchronous and offline-capable.
steps.say: So the first thing to understand about Zero is that a query is answered locally and instantly. The network is something that happens later, in the background.

chapters.title: Bring Your Own Postgres
chapters.blurb: Zero never replaces your database; it opens a logical replication slot and mirrors your Postgres into a fast SQLite replica.

story.title: Bring Your Own Postgres
story.subtitle: Local-first reads, your own Postgres, and live queries on every platform

nodes.label: Your Postgres
nodes.sublabel: your own DB · source of truth

steps.title: Bring Your Own Postgres
steps.narration: Your existing **Postgres** stays the source of truth. `zero-cache` connects to it and keeps a live copy it can serve from.
steps.say: So where does the data really live? In your own Postgres. Zero never takes that away from you.
steps.coverSubtitle: Zero doesn't replace your database — it mirrors it

steps.title: A logical replication slot
steps.narration: The **`PostgresChangeSource`** subscribes to Postgres **logical replication**, decoding the write-ahead log via `pgoutput` and tracking position by **LSN**.
steps.say: Your existing Postgres stays the single source of truth. Zero connects to it as a replication client and opens a logical replication slot, the same mechanism Postgres uses to feed a read replica.

steps.title: An ordered change log
steps.narration: The **`ChangeStreamer`** records each change into one durable, ordered log — the canonical sequence every replica replays from.
steps.say: Every insert, update and delete arrives as a change event. The change streamer writes them into a single ordered log, so nothing is lost and everything stays in order.

steps.title: The replicator applies changes
steps.narration: The **`ReplicatorService`** subscribes to the change log and applies each change in order, advancing the replica's version.
steps.say: The replicator subscribes to that log and applies each change in sequence.

steps.title: Into the SQLite replica
steps.narration: Changes land in the **replica** — a SQLite file managed by `zqlite`'s **`Database`** (`@rocicorp/zero-sqlite3`), set up by `setupReplica()`.
steps.say: It writes them into a SQLite database that Zero calls the replica: a fast, local mirror of your Postgres, built on the zqlite engine.

steps.title: Acknowledge the position
steps.narration: An **`Acker`** confirms the applied **LSN** upstream, so the slot can be advanced and replication resumes precisely on restart.
steps.say: As it goes it acknowledges its position back to Postgres, so replication can always resume exactly where it left off.

steps.title: Postgres in, replica out
steps.narration: Ingestion spine: **Postgres** → **`ChangeSource`** → **`ChangeStreamer`** → **`Replicator`** → **SQLite replica**. The replica is a cache, never the source of truth.
steps.say: The picture so far: your Postgres is the truth, and zero cache keeps a live SQLite mirror of it that it can query at memory speed.

chapters.title: The View-Syncer
chapters.blurb: How one query stays live: the view-syncer runs it against the replica, remembers what each client has seen, and pokes down only the diff.

story.title: The View-Syncer
story.subtitle: Local-first reads, your own Postgres, and live queries on every platform

steps.title: The View-Syncer
steps.narration: The **`ViewSyncerService`** is the server component that keeps each client's query result current as the replica changes.
steps.say: Now the heart of Zero: the part that keeps your local result in sync with the replica, sending only what actually changed.
steps.coverSubtitle: How one query stays live, sending only what changed

steps.title: Query plus a cookie
steps.narration: Over a websocket, the client sends its query and a **cookie** (its last version). A **`ClientHandler`** in the **`ViewSyncer`** tracks that connection.
steps.say: The Zero client holds a websocket open to a server component called the view syncer. It sends up its query, along with a cookie marking the last version it has seen.

steps.title: Run it on the replica
steps.narration: The **`PipelineDriver`** executes the ZQL pipeline against the **replica**, streaming matching rows as `RowAdd` changes.
steps.say: The view syncer runs that query through a pipeline driver, the server side incremental view engine, reading the matching rows straight from the SQLite replica.

steps.title: Remember what was sent
steps.narration: The **`CVRStore`** persists a **client view record** (`CVR`) in Postgres — the per-client set of queries and rows already delivered.
steps.say: It records exactly which rows this client has been sent, in a client view record, or CVR, stored back in Postgres. That is Zero's memory of what every client already has.

steps.title: The first poke
steps.narration: The initial result ships as a **poke** — `PokeStartMessage`, one or more `PokePartMessage` (carrying `rowsPatch`), then `PokeEndMessage`.
steps.say: For the first sync it streams the whole result down to the client as a poke: a start message, the rows in the middle, and an end message.

steps.title: Incremental recompute
steps.narration: When the replica advances, the **`PipelineDriver`** emits just the affected `RowAdd` / `RowRemove` / `RowEdit` deltas — no full re-scan.
steps.say: Later, a write lands in the replica. The pipeline driver feels that change and incrementally recomputes only the rows that moved in or out of your query.

steps.title: Poke only the diff
steps.narration: It diffs against the stored **`CVR`** and sends only a **`rowsPatch`** in the next `PokePart` — minimal bytes for each change.
steps.say: The view syncer compares that against the client's CVR, and pokes down just the difference: a tiny rows patch instead of the whole list.

steps.title: Live, with minimal traffic
steps.narration: Sync loop: **query + cookie** → run on **replica** → record in **CVR** → **poke** the diff. Subscribe once, then receive patches forever.
steps.say: That is the loop that makes Zero feel instant and stay cheap: query once, then receive a steady trickle of patches as the world changes.

chapters.title: Writes & Drizzle
chapters.blurb: A mutation is optimistic on the client, then runs as a real transaction on your server — through Drizzle, Kysely, Prisma or plain Postgres.

story.title: Writes & Drizzle
story.subtitle: Local-first reads, your own Postgres, and live queries on every platform

steps.title: Writes & Drizzle
steps.narration: Writes go through **custom mutators**. Zero applies them optimistically on the client, then runs them for real on your server.
steps.say: Reads are only half the story. Let's follow a write, and see where Drizzle fits in.
steps.coverSubtitle: Optimistic on the client, authoritative on your server

steps.title: Call mutate
steps.narration: You call **`z.mutate.issue.update(...)`**. The **`Zero`** client runs the mutator's client function immediately — an *optimistic* update.
steps.say: When you change something you call mutate on the Zero client. Zero applies it optimistically, as if it had already succeeded.

steps.title: Instant local write
steps.narration: The mutation writes into the **`IDBStore`** the UI already reads from, so `useQuery` results update synchronously — *zero* perceived latency.
steps.say: The change is written into the same local store the UI reads from, so your screen updates the instant you act. No round trip.

steps.title: Push to your server
steps.narration: Asynchronously, the mutation is pushed to **server mutators** on your API server (e.g. via `zero-pg`), which hold the authoritative logic.
steps.say: In the background Zero pushes that mutation to your own server, where it runs against the real database through a server mutator you write.

steps.title: This is where Drizzle fits
steps.narration: Wrap your DB with the **`DrizzleConnection`** adapter (`zero-server/src/adapters/drizzle.ts`). Adapters also exist for `kysely`, `prisma`, `pg` and `postgresjs`.
steps.say: And this is where Drizzle comes in. Zero ships a Drizzle adapter, so your mutator can talk to Postgres through your existing Drizzle schema. Kysely, Prisma and plain Postgres adapters are there too.

steps.title: The authoritative write
steps.narration: The adapter opens a **`DrizzleTransaction`** and commits to your **Postgres** — the real, durable write. The optimistic copy is reconciled once it lands.
steps.say: The adapter runs your mutation as a real transaction against your Postgres. The authoritative write actually happens here.

steps.title: The write becomes a change
steps.narration: Once committed, the write is an ordinary Postgres change: it re-enters via the **`ChangeSource`** and the **`ViewSyncer`** pokes it to every subscribed client.
steps.say: From there it closes the circle. That committed write is just another Postgres change, so it flows back through replication and the view syncer pokes it out to every other client.

chapters.title: One Query, Every Platform
chapters.blurb: The same sync engine powers React, Solid and React Native — including a native SDK that persists to on-device SQLite.

story.title: One Query, Every Platform
story.subtitle: Local-first reads, your own Postgres, and live queries on every platform

steps.title: One Query, Every Platform
steps.narration: One core (`zero-client`) drives every binding: **`zero-react`**, **`zero-solid`**, and **`zero-react-native`**.
steps.say: Finally, the whole picture, because the same engine drives every front end Zero supports.
steps.coverSubtitle: The same sync engine behind React, Solid and React Native

steps.title: The spine you've met
steps.narration: **Postgres** → **`zero-cache`** (replica + `ViewSyncerService`) → **`Zero`** client. The client keeps the materialized, always-current result.
steps.say: Here is the spine you've already met: your Postgres on the left, zero cache mirroring and serving it in the middle, and the Zero client holding the live result on the device.

steps.title: React
steps.narration: **`zero-react`** exports **`useQuery`** and **`useSuspenseQuery`** for live data, plus **`useZero`** and **`ZeroProvider`** for client access.
steps.say: For React, the zero react package gives you hooks: use query for live data, and use zero to reach the client, wrapped in a zero provider.

steps.title: Solid
steps.narration: **`zero-solid`** exports **`useQuery`** (and `createQuery`) returning a Solid `Accessor` signal, plus `useZero` / `createUseZero`.
steps.say: For Solid, zero solid offers the same use query, returning a reactive signal that slots naturally into Solid's reactivity.

steps.title: Native SDK
steps.narration: **`zero-react-native`** exports **`expoSQLiteStoreProvider`**, swapping IndexedDB for on-device SQLite via `expo-sqlite` (an `op-sqlite` provider also exists).
steps.say: And yes, there are native SDKs. The zero react native package runs the very same client on a phone, persisting to on-device SQLite through Expo's SQLite store.

steps.title: The whole loop
steps.narration: End to end: **Postgres** (truth) → **`zero-cache`** (replica + view-syncer, patches) → **`Zero`** client → **React / Solid / React Native**. Local-first, always in sync.
steps.say: So that's Zero, end to end: your Postgres stays the source of truth, zero cache mirrors it and syncs live queries as patches, and React, Solid or React Native render a result that's already on the device.
